chapter_theme: On the day of Puhar's festival, Chithirapathi, grieved that Madhavi and Manimekalai stay away, sends Vayantamalai to tell Madhavi that the town calls an accomplished dancer's turn to tapas shameful. Madhavi answers that she lost her shame when she outlived the news of her lover's suffering, that Kannaki fits none of the known kinds of pathini, that Manimekalai as Kannaki's daughter will go to tapas and never to the courtesan's trade, and that the Buddhist teacher Aravanar has taught her that birth is suffering born of attachment and given her the five precepts.

cast.role: Madhavi's mother, a senior courtesan of Puhar
Madhavi's attendant and companion, the Silappathikaram's வசந்தமாலை
the courtesan dancer, Kovalan's lover and Manimekalai's mother, now turned to tapas
the many of Puhar who talk about Madhavi's renunciation
Kovalan's wife, the great pathini who burned Madurai, named here only by that title
the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, later in Kanchi, in whose dwelling Madhavi has taken refuge

manimekalai:2:1-16.reading: On the festival day of the island's peace rite for the king of the gods, Chithirapathi, pained that Madhavi and Manimekalai have not come, calls her daughter's friend Vayantamalai and tells her to go and tell them what the town is saying; Vayantamalai, herself wasted by Madhavi's renunciation, goes to the flower hall where the two sit, grieves at the dancer's worn body, and begins to speak.
manimekalai:2:1-16.nuance: Chithirapathi does not plead; she sends the town's gossip (அலர்) as her argument, so public talk is the pressure brought to bear on a renunciant. Both women who come to Madhavi are wasted by her choice (அயர்ந்து, மெய் வாடிய; வாடிய மேனி), the friend in grief and Madhavi in austerity.
manimekalai:2:1-16.event: Chithirapathi, grieved that Madhavi stays away from the festival, sends Vayantamalai to tell her the town's talk, and Vayantamalai comes to Madhavi in the flower hall.

manimekalai:2:17-33.reading: Vayantamalai reports what the town says of Madhavi: that a woman who learned and mastered every art laid down for dancing women, the court and common styles of dance and song, the lute, drum and flute, the arts of the ball, cookery, perfume, bathing, the bed, the seasons, the body, reading intent, speech, cipher, painting, garlands, adornment, the reckoning of time and the treatises, should have taken up tapas is a shame.
manimekalai:2:17-33.nuance: The list is the town's argument, not an ornament: every accomplishment named is a reason, in its eyes, that the dancer belongs to her trade. நல் தவம் (33) is the town's own phrase, so it grants the tapas is good and calls it shameful for her. Several items (கரந்து உறை கணக்கு, வட்டிகைச் செய்தி, கோவையின் கோப்பு) are rare names of arts and are taken here only as items of the list. The claim is answered at once: Vayantamalai herself sets it down to the talk of the many (34-36), and Madhavi replies to it in 38-57, which is why its stance is refuted.
manimekalai:2:17-33.event: Vayantamalai tells Madhavi that the town says her turning to tapas, after mastering the dancer's arts, is shameful.

claims.claim: a woman trained in the arts of the dancing women shames herself by taking up tapas

manimekalai:2:34-41.unit_note: The core unit 34-56 is split at 41, where Madhavi's first sentence closes on நாணுத் துறந்தேன்; 42 opens her account of the kinds of pathini.
manimekalai:2:34-41.reading: Vayantamalai sets the words, 'there is no good in it, it is shameful', down to the ill-bred talk of the many rather than the worthy elders of the old city, and Madhavi answers that she, who stayed alive on hearing of her lover's cruel suffering, already lost the town's good word and gave up her shame.
manimekalai:2:34-41.nuance: Madhavi turns the town's charge: the shame is not in her tapas but in her having outlived Kovalan's death (போதல்செய்யா உயிரொடு நின்றே), so renunciation is her answer to a shame already incurred. Whether lines 34 to 36 are Vayantamalai's own gloss on the town's words or part of the report is not certain; the reading takes them as hers, since 37 names her as the one who spoke.
manimekalai:2:34-41.event: Vayantamalai disowns the town's talk as the many's, and Madhavi replies that she gave up shame when she survived the news of her lover's suffering.

claims.claim: a woman who stays alive on hearing of her beloved's suffering has given up her shame

manimekalai:2:42-57.unit_note: Starts at 42 after the split at 41, and runs to 57, where the sentence begun at 55 (மணிமேகலை அருந் தவப் படுத்தல் அல்லது) closes on படாஅள்; the core unit 57-75 began mid-sentence.
manimekalai:2:42-57.reading: Madhavi says that pathini women of the wide world, when their husbands die, give up their lives with sighs like a smith's bellows, or else enter the blazing fire as if a cool pool, or else wear down the body in vows to live again with the beloved, but that Kannaki was of none of these kinds: unable to bear her husband's suffering she twisted off her breast and set the king's city aflame, and Manimekalai, the daughter of that great pathini, will be brought to tapas and never to the evil trade of unreformed conduct.
manimekalai:2:42-57.nuance: Madhavi calls Manimekalai the daughter (மகள்) of the great pathini, not her own, so the courtesan's daughter is given Kannaki's lineage and with it a claim to be kept from the courtesan's trade (தீத் தொழில்). The three kinds are ranked by the word ஆயின் (if not), each a fallback from the one before; the third does not say in which life the couple will live together. Madhavi herself fits none of the three either, having lived on, which is the point of her opening in 38 to 41. The second kind, who enters the fire as if it were a cool pool (45), uses the figure of Purananuru 246, and the third, who wears the body down in vows, is the widow's austerity that the queen of that poem refuses.
manimekalai:2:42-57.event: Madhavi tells Vayantamalai the kinds of pathini, sets Kannaki apart from them, and says Manimekalai will be given to tapas.

claims.claim: a chaste wife dies at her husband's death, or enters the fire, or wears down her body in vows to rejoin him
the daughter of a great pathini must be given to tapas and not to the courtesan's trade

manimekalai:2:58-75.unit_note: Starts at 58 (ஆங்கனம் அன்றியும், 'besides that') after the boundary moved from 56/57 to 57/58.
manimekalai:2:58-75.reading: Madhavi tells how she came to this dwelling of ascetics and fell at the feet of the teacher Aravanar, told him her lover's suffering, and was taught that the born meet ever-growing suffering and the unborn the greatest bliss, that the one comes of attachment and the other to those who are free of it, and was shown the five precepts as the way to be saved; she bids Vayantamalai tell this to the courtesans and to Chithirapathi, and Vayantamalai leaves helpless, like one who has dropped a rare gem into the sea.
manimekalai:2:58-75.nuance: The teaching answers grief, not a question of doctrine: Madhavi brings Aravanar her lover's suffering and is given the cause of all suffering. ஐவகைச் சீலம் are the five lay precepts of the Buddhists, offered as உய் வகை, a way of survival, before any word of release. The closing simile makes Madhavi, lost to the courtesans, the gem dropped in the sea.
manimekalai:2:58-75.event: Madhavi tells how Aravanar taught her the cause of suffering and the five precepts and sends word to Chithirapathi; Vayantamalai goes away in despair.

claims.claim: those who are born meet growing suffering and those not born meet the greatest bliss
suffering comes from attachment and bliss is reached by those freed of it
the five precepts are the way to be saved

links.note: The town lists the arts set down for dancing women that Madhavi mastered; Silappathikaram 3 opens on her seven years' training in dance, song and beauty for her first performance before the king.
links.teaches: The training that the earlier epic presents as the making of Madhavi's fame becomes in the town's mouth its argument against her leaving that life, so the courtesan's accomplishments bind her to her trade as a claim others hold on her.

links.note: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life rather than shame for life; Madhavi says that by staying alive after hearing of her lover's suffering she gave up her shame.
links.teaches: Read against the couplet, Madhavi's confession places her among those who kept life at the cost of shame, so the shame the town sees in her tapas already lay in her survival, and her renunciation becomes the answer of one who has failed the rule rather than a new disgrace.

gains.a: the general rule that makes her confession intelligible: the couplet says why outliving the news of Kovalan's suffering counts as giving up shame
gains.b: a person who has failed the rule and lives on, which shows a way of answering lost shame, by tapas, that the couplet's choice between shame and death leaves out

links.note: Madhavi recounts Kannaki twisting off her breast and setting the king's city aflame; Silappathikaram 21 tells the act.
links.teaches: Madhavi retells the burning as the deed of the mother she assigns to Manimekalai, so the earlier epic's vengeance becomes a lineage by which a courtesan's daughter is claimed for tapas instead of her mother's trade.

links.note: Perunkoppendu tells the elders holding her back that for her, her husband dead, a lotus pond and the pyre's fire are one, and scorns the widow's life of sparse food and bare ground; Madhavi's second kind of pathini enters the blazing fire as into a cool-water pool, and her third wears the body down in vows.
links.teaches: The queen's single act of defiance, in which the pyre is a cool pond and the austere widowhood she refuses is worse than fire, becomes in the epic a ranked typology of the chaste wife where entering the fire is only the second kind and the vowed austerity she despised is admitted as the third, and all three are then set beneath Kannaki.

gains.a: the source of the fire-as-cool-pool figure in a widow's own speech against the elders, so that Madhavi's kinds are seen to be drawn from remembered acts and not invented as a scheme
gains.b: a later frame in which the queen's choice is one recognised option among three, with the widow's austerity she scorned now counted as a path of chastity, which shows how the poem's personal refusal was absorbed into a norm

links.note: Madhavi says Manimekalai will be brought to great tapas and never to the courtesan's trade; at the close of kaathai 30 Manimekalai takes up tapas and vows to end the course of births.
links.teaches: The mother's claim made for her daughter in the third kaathai is fulfilled only in the last, and by the daughter's own vow after hearing the whole doctrine, so the epic runs between a claim made over Manimekalai and her own assent to it.

links.note: Aravanar's four lines to Madhavi set suffering for the born, bliss for the unborn and attachment as the cause; in kaathai 30 he sets out the twelve links, with attachment (பற்றே) one link among them, and says the born who know them gain the great reward.
links.teaches: The same teacher gives the grieving mother a single cause and five precepts, and the daughter the full twelve-link chain, so the epic shows the doctrine scaled to its hearer: consolation and lay discipline first, the analysis of release later.

links.note: Kural 349 says that when attachment ends it cuts off births; Aravanar says suffering comes from attachment, bliss to those free of it, and that birth itself brings growing suffering.
links.teaches: The couplet ties the end of attachment to the end of rebirth but sets no value on birth; Aravanar's lines add that birth is itself suffering and offer a bereaved lay woman five precepts as the way in, not the renouncer's clean cut.

gains.a: a bare causal statement, attachment to rebirth, against which the teacher's added judgment that birth is suffering stands out as the Buddhist addition
gains.b: a scene where its renouncer's rule is given as consolation to a grieving woman still in the world, with lay precepts as the first step

links.note: Tirumular says the Lord who made birth for joy shut it in the suffering of the bond; Aravanar says the born meet growing suffering, the unborn great bliss, and suffering comes from attachment.
links.teaches: Both trace suffering to a binding, attachment or the bond, but they disagree about birth itself: for the Buddhist teacher birth is the suffering and not being born is bliss, while for Tirumular birth was made for joy and the bond was laid on it by the same Lord; the conflict holds on reading இன்பப் பிறவி as birth made for joy.

gains.a: a theist account in which a maker lays the suffering on birth, which shows that Aravanar names no maker and makes attachment alone the cause
gains.b: an opposed claim that birth is itself suffering, which shows that the verse's birth made for joy is a position taken, not common ground
